name: P2 · Unit 4 — Programming Languages & Web
description: 4 of 9 topics so far (11 sets × 30 questions): Language Design and Translation Issues; Elementary Data Types; Programming in C – Part 1; Programming in C – Part 2. More topics are added to this pack as the plan goes on; re-importing only adds the new sets.

sets.name: 1 · Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments

questions.question: A program in which computation is expressed as facts and rules, and execution consists of answering queries, belongs to which paradigm?
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Logic languages such as Prolog state facts and rules; the system answers queries by inference.

questions.question: The imperative paradigm is characterised mainly by:

options.D: Statements that change program state through assignment

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Imperative languages mirror the von Neumann machine: variables are memory cells updated by assignment.

questions.question: Referential transparency, a key property of pure functional languages, means that:

options.A: Pointers are always visible to the programmer
options.B: An expression can be replaced by its value without changing the program's behaviour
options.D: Variables can be reassigned many times

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: With no side effects, f(x) always gives the same value, so it can be substituted by that value.

questions.question: Which language is primarily a pure functional language?
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Haskell is a lazy, purely functional language; the others are imperative.

questions.question: Functional programming languages are based on which formal model of computation?
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Church's lambda calculus underlies LISP, ML and Haskell; logic languages are based on predicate calculus.

questions.question: The 'von Neumann bottleneck' refers to:

options.B: The limit on the number of registers in a CPU
options.D: The limited speed of transfer between memory and the CPU, which shaped imperative languages

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Instructions and data travel through one path between memory and processor; imperative languages model this cell-by-cell style.

questions.question: Orthogonality in programming-language design means:

options.A: Every construct has exactly one syntax
options.B: A small set of primitive constructs can be combined in a small number of ways, and every combination is legal and meaningful
options.C: Programs run on every hardware platform
options.D: The language has no reserved words

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Orthogonal features combine freely without special exceptions (Sebesta; Pratt: 'orthogonality').

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Readability and writability of a language can conflict with each other.
II. Making a language more and more orthogonal without limit always improves it.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Too much orthogonality creates many useless combinations (ALGOL 68 is the classic example), so II is false.

questions.question: Which language feature most directly reduces program reliability?

options.C: Aliasing – two or more names for the same memory cell

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Aliasing lets a change through one name silently change another; the other features improve reliability.

questions.question: In C, the binding of a variable to its data type occurs at:
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: C is statically typed: types are bound by declarations when the program is compiled.

questions.question: The binding of the symbol '*' to the multiplication operation takes place at:
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Operator symbols get their meaning when the language is defined.

questions.question: Java is usually implemented as a:

options.A: Hybrid system: source compiled to bytecode, which a JVM interprets or JIT-compiles
options.C: Pure compiler to native code only

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: javac produces platform-independent bytecode; the JVM interprets it or compiles hot code just-in-time.

questions.question: Compared with compilation, pure interpretation has which main disadvantage?

options.D: Much slower execution, because each statement is decoded every time it runs

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Decoding high-level statements repeatedly makes interpretation typically 10–100 times slower (Sebesta).

questions.question: A 'virtual computer' in Pratt's layered view is:

options.A: A computer simulated only on paper
options.C: Hardware together with the software layers (OS, translators) that together behave like a machine executing the language

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Each layer of software on top of hardware presents a more convenient 'virtual machine' to the layer above.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT normally a component of a programming environment?

options.D: The arithmetic-logic unit of the target CPU

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: A programming environment is the set of software tools (editors, debuggers, verifiers, test tools) used while developing programs.

questions.question: For separate compilation of a subprogram, the compiler needs to know:

options.A: The specifications (interfaces) of the other subprograms it calls
options.C: The complete source code of every other subprogram
options.D: The run-time values of all variables

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Header files/prototypes give the needed interface information; the linker later joins the separately compiled pieces.

questions.question: Programs in an embedded-system environment differ most from batch programs in that they:

options.C: Often have real-time constraints and must run without human intervention

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Embedded software controls devices and must respond within time limits, reliably and autonomously.

questions.question:
Match the paradigm with a typical language:
a. Imperative
b. Functional
c. Logic
d. Object-oriented

1. Smalltalk
2. C
3. LISP
4. Prolog
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: C – imperative; LISP – functional; Prolog – logic; Smalltalk – pure object-oriented.

questions.question:
Match the language with its main original purpose or feature:
a. FORTRAN
b. COBOL
c. LISP
d. ALGOL 60

1. Business data processing
2. Scientific computation
3. First language defined using BNF
4. List processing and AI
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: FORTRAN (1957) – scientific; COBOL (1960) – business; LISP (1958) – list processing/AI; ALGOL 60 – syntax described in BNF.

questions.question: The concepts of class and object were first introduced in:
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Simula 67 (Dahl and Nygaard) introduced classes for simulation; Smalltalk and C++ came later.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Pure functional programs are comparatively easy to evaluate in parallel.
Reason (R): Without side effects, independent sub-expressions can be evaluated in any order.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Since evaluation order cannot change results, independent parts can safely run in parallel.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Java bytecode can run on any machine that has a Java Virtual Machine.
Reason (R): The Java compiler translates source code directly into the native machine code of the target processor.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: javac produces bytecode, not native code – that is exactly why it is portable.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): C is a strongly typed language in the strict sense.
Reason (R): C allows unions and implicit conversions that are not type-checked.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Because of unchecked unions, casts and coercions, C is not strongly typed; R is true and shows why A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): COBOL is widely used for business data processing.
Reason (R): COBOL was designed by a committee (CODASYL) around 1959–60.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Both are true, but being designed by a committee does not explain its use in business; its record handling and English-like syntax do.

questions.question: A language in which the order of statement execution is decided mainly by user actions such as clicks and key presses follows the:
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Event-driven programs wait for events and run handlers; common in GUIs and JavaScript.

questions.question:
Consider the statements about scripting languages such as Python and JavaScript:
I. They are usually interpreted (or compiled to bytecode at run time).
II. They are usually dynamically typed.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Both statements describe typical scripting languages.

questions.question: SQL is best described as:

options.A: A declarative language – the user states what data is wanted, not how to get it
options.B: An imperative language with loops over files
options.C: A logic language based on backtracking

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: The query optimiser decides the access strategy; the programmer only specifies the result.

questions.question: Which statement about compilers and interpreters is INCORRECT?

options.B: A compiler translates the whole program before it runs
options.C: An interpreter can give error messages close to the source statement
options.D: An interpreter produces an object program that is saved for later execution

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: An interpreter executes directly and does not save an object program; a compiler does.

questions.question: Which is NOT one of the essential features of object-oriented programming?
questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Sebesta lists abstract data types, inheritance and dynamic binding; pointer arithmetic has nothing to do with OOP.

questions.question: Which of the following contributes most to the 'cost of use' of a language, as discussed by Pratt?

options.A: Costs of program execution, translation, creation/testing and maintenance together
options.B: Only the price of the compiler licence
options.C: Only the cost of the hardware
options.D: Only the time to type the program

questions.subject: Language Concepts, Paradigms, Models and Programming Environments
questions.explanation: Pratt lists execution, translation, program creation/testing/use and maintenance as the costs of using a language.

questions.question: The syntax of a programming language specifies:

options.D: The form or structure of expressions, statements and program units

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Syntax = form; semantics = meaning.

questions.question: The output of the lexical analyser is:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: The scanner groups characters into lexemes and passes tokens to the parser.

questions.question: In C, a missing semicolon at the end of a statement is detected during:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Each character is a valid token; it is the sequence of tokens that violates the grammar.

questions.question: An error such as adding an integer to a structure variable in C is detected during:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: The statement may be syntactically correct; the type rules are checked in semantic analysis.

questions.question: Information about identifiers – their names, types and scopes – collected during translation is stored in the:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: The symbol table is built and used by all phases of the translator.

questions.question: In BNF (Backus–Naur Form), the symbol ::= means:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: <expr> ::= <expr> + <term> reads 'expr is defined as expr + term'.

questions.question: BNF was first used to describe the syntax of:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: John Backus and Peter Naur used it in the ALGOL 60 report.

questions.question: Extended BNF (EBNF) adds which notations?

options.A: { } for repetition and [ ] for optional parts

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: EBNF makes grammars shorter; it does not describe more languages than BNF.

questions.question: A grammar is ambiguous if:

options.B: It has more than one start symbol
options.D: Some sentence has two or more distinct parse trees

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Equivalently, some sentence has two distinct leftmost derivations.

questions.question: With the grammar E → E + E | E * E | id, how many distinct parse trees does id + id * id have?
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Either + or * can be the root operator: (id + id) * id or id + (id * id).

questions.question: With the ambiguous grammar E → E + E | id, how many distinct parse trees does id + id + id + id have?
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Three operators can be bracketed in Catalan(3) = 5 ways.

questions.question: In an unambiguous expression grammar, an operator of higher precedence is placed:

options.A: Nowhere – precedence cannot be expressed in grammars
options.B: At a lower level of the grammar, so it appears nearer the leaves of the parse tree

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: E → E + T, T → T * F: * is generated lower in the tree, so it binds tighter and is evaluated first.

questions.question: A left-recursive rule such as E → E − T | T gives the operator − :
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: a − b − c is parsed as (a − b) − c.

questions.question: How many tokens are in the C statement:  sum = sum + x * 10;
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: sum, =, sum, +, x, *, 10, ; → 8 tokens.

questions.question: How many tokens are in the C statement:  printf("%d", a);
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: printf, (, "%d", ',', a, ), ; → 7 tokens; a string literal is a single token.

questions.question: Which of the following belongs to the synthesis part of translation?
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Analysis breaks down the source; synthesis (optimisation and code generation) builds the object program.

questions.question: Resolving external references between separately compiled modules is done by the:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: The linker combines object modules and library routines into one executable.

questions.question: Relocation, done by a relocating loader or linker, means:

options.A: Rewriting the program in another language
options.B: Moving the source file to another folder
options.C: Adjusting addresses in object code so the program can run at a location different from the one assumed at translation

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Address-sensitive words are modified by the load (relocation) address.

questions.question: Replacing  x * 2  by  x + x  or  x << 1  is an example of:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: An expensive operation is replaced by a cheaper equivalent one.

questions.question: Evaluating  3 * 4  at compile time and using 12 in the object code is called:
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Expressions with constant operands are computed by the compiler itself.

questions.question: A cross-compiler is a compiler that:

options.A: Translates between two high-level languages only
options.D: Runs on one machine and produces code for a different machine

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Used to build software for embedded devices from a desktop computer.

questions.question:
Match the phase with its main output:
a. Lexical analyser
b. Parser
c. Semantic analyser
d. Code generator

1. Target code
2. Tokens
3. Parse tree
4. Type-checked (annotated) tree
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Tokens → parse tree → annotated tree → target code.

questions.question:
Match the error with the phase that normally detects it:
a. Illegal character @ in an identifier
b. Unbalanced parentheses
c. Use of an undeclared variable
d. Division by zero with values read at run time

1. Syntax analysis
2. Lexical analysis
3. Execution
4. Semantic analysis
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Characters → lexical; structure → syntax; declarations/types → semantic; values known only at run time → execution.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Comments and white space are removed during lexical analysis.
Reason (R): They do not affect the meaning of the program.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Because they carry no meaning for later phases, the scanner discards them.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A context-free grammar can express every syntactic restriction of C.
Reason (R): The rule 'a variable must be declared before it is used' is context-sensitive.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Declare-before-use cannot be expressed by a CFG, so such rules are checked as static semantics; A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Syntax diagrams (railroad diagrams) are an alternative to BNF.
Reason (R): The syntax of Pascal was popularised using syntax diagrams.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Both are true, but Pascal's use of them does not explain why they are an alternative notation.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Lexical analysers are usually built from finite automata.
Reason (R): The tokens of most languages can be described only by context-sensitive grammars.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: tokens are described by regular expressions, which is why finite automata suffice.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Every regular language is context-free.
II. Every context-free language is regular.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Regular ⊂ context-free; {aⁿbⁿ} is context-free but not regular.

questions.question: In C, in the statement  if (a) if (b) s1; else s2;  the else is associated with:

options.D: Neither – it is a syntax error

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: The 'dangling else' is resolved by matching the nearest unmatched if.

questions.question: Attribute grammars are mainly used to describe:

options.C: Static semantics, such as type compatibility rules

questions.subject: Syntax and Stages in Translation
questions.explanation: Attributes attached to grammar symbols carry types and other information checked during semantic analysis.

questions.question:
Match the grammar type (Chomsky hierarchy) with its recognising machine:
a. Type 0 (unrestricted)
b. Type 1 (context-sensitive)
c. Type 2 (context-free)
d. Type 3 (regular)

1. Linear bounded automaton
2. Turing machine
3. Pushdown automaton
4. Finite automaton
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: TM ⊃ LBA ⊃ PDA ⊃ FA, matching types 0 to 3.

questions.question: In a deterministic finite automaton (DFA):

options.C: There may be several next states for the same input
options.D: For each state and each input symbol there is exactly one next state

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Determinism = one unique transition per (state, symbol).

questions.question: An NFA with 4 states is converted to a DFA by subset construction. The DFA can have at most:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Each DFA state is a subset of the NFA's states: at most 2⁴ = 16.

questions.question: The transition function of an NFA (without ε-moves) is:

options.B: δ: Q × Σ × Γ → Q × Γ*

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: It maps a state and a symbol to a set of states; the last option is a PDA's.

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA over {0,1} accepting all strings whose length is divisible by 3 is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: States track length mod 3: 0, 1, 2.

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA over {0,1} accepting all strings that end in 01 is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: States: nothing useful seen, last symbol 0, last two symbols 01 (accepting).

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA over {a,b} accepting strings with exactly two a's is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Counts 0, 1, 2 a's plus a dead state for more than two.

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA over {0,1} accepting strings whose second-last symbol is 1 is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: The DFA must remember the last two symbols: 2² = 4 states.

questions.question: The regular expression (a+b)*abb denotes:

options.A: All strings over {a,b} ending in abb
options.D: All strings containing exactly one abb

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Any prefix (a+b)* followed by abb.

questions.question: How many strings of length 3 over {a,b} are in the language of a*b*?
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: aaa, aab, abb, bbb – some a's followed by some b's.

questions.question: Which of the following languages is NOT regular?

options.C: Strings over {a,b} with an even number of a's

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Matching counts needs unbounded memory; the pumping lemma proves aⁿbⁿ is not regular.

questions.question: The language { aⁿbⁿcⁿ | n ≥ 1 } is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: A single stack cannot match three counts; an LBA can.

questions.question: The language { wwᴿ | w ∈ {a,b}* } (even-length palindromes) is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: An NPDA must guess the middle; no DPDA can accept it.

questions.question: The language generated by S → aSb | ε is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Each step adds one a on the left and one b on the right.

questions.question: The grammar S → aS | bS | a generates:

options.A: All strings over {a,b} that end in a
options.B: All strings that start with a

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Any sequence of a/b followed finally by a.

questions.question: In a context-sensitive grammar every production α → β satisfies:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Non-contracting productions define type-1 grammars.

questions.question: A Moore machine differs from a Mealy machine in that its output depends on:

options.C: The current state and current input

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Mealy output is attached to transitions (state + input).

questions.question: For an input string of length n, a Moore machine produces an output string of length:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: It outputs once in the start state and once after each input symbol.

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA over {0,1} accepting all strings that contain at least one 1 is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: One state for 'no 1 seen yet' and one accepting state that loops on 0 and 1.

questions.question: Which regular expression is NOT equivalent to (a+b)*?
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: (ab)* cannot generate 'a' or 'ba'; the others generate every string over {a,b}.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Deterministic pushdown automata accept every context-free language.
II. Every regular language is accepted by some deterministic pushdown automaton.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: DPDAs are weaker than NPDAs (wwᴿ), but a DPDA can simply ignore its stack and act as a DFA.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Context-free languages are closed under union.
II. Context-free languages are closed under intersection.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: aⁿbⁿcᵐ ∩ aᵐbⁿcⁿ = aⁿbⁿcⁿ, which is not context-free, so II is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Every DFA is also an NFA.
Reason (R): A DFA is simply an NFA in which each transition leads to exactly one state.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: The definition of an NFA includes the deterministic case.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A finite automaton can recognise the language of balanced parentheses.
Reason (R): A finite automaton has only a finite amount of memory in the form of its states.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Nesting depth is unbounded, so a finite automaton cannot count it; R is true and explains why A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): NFAs and DFAs accept exactly the same class of languages.
Reason (R): An NFA may have more than one transition for the same state and input symbol.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Both true, but R describes nondeterminism; the equivalence follows from subset construction.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The halting problem for Turing machines is undecidable.
Reason (R): Turing machines are less powerful than pushdown automata.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: A is true (Turing, 1936). R is false: Turing machines are the most powerful of these models.

questions.question: Left-linear and right-linear grammars generate exactly the:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Linear grammars with the non-terminal at one end correspond to finite automata.

questions.question: In compilers, finite automata and pushdown automata are used respectively for:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: Tokens are regular; program structure is context-free.

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA over {a,b} accepting all strings of length at least 2 is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: States for length 0, length 1 and length ≥ 2 (accepting, looping).

questions.question: The minimum number of states of a DFA that accepts binary numbers (read from the most significant bit) divisible by 3 is:
questions.subject: Formal Transition Models
questions.explanation: States track the value mod 3; reading bit b moves r to (2r + b) mod 3.

questions.question: In Pratt's terminology, a data object is:

options.B: A class in an object-oriented language only
options.C: A constant written in the source program
options.D: A run-time grouping of one or more pieces of data – a container for data values

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: A data object is a location (container); a data value is what it holds.

questions.question: In the C assignment  x = x + 1;  the x on the left-hand side denotes its:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: The left side needs a location to store into; the right side uses x's current value.

questions.question: The lifetime of a data object is:

options.A: The time taken to compile it
options.C: The number of lines in which its name is visible
options.D: The period of execution during which it exists and is bound to storage

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Lifetime is temporal; scope is textual visibility.

questions.question: Which group of languages relies mainly on dynamic type checking?
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: In these languages types belong to values and are checked when operations execute.

questions.question: A language is called strongly typed if:

options.A: It allows no conversions at all
options.B: All type errors are always detected, either at compile time or at run time
options.C: Every variable must be declared at the start of the program
options.D: It has at least ten built-in types

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Strong typing = no type error goes undetected (Sebesta).

questions.question: Coercion is:

options.A: An implicit type conversion inserted automatically by the translator
options.C: An explicit cast written by the programmer

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: In 2 + 3.5, C coerces 2 to double.

questions.question: In C, what is the value of  (float)(7 / 2) ?
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: 7 / 2 is integer division = 3, which is then converted to 3.0.

questions.question: In C, after  int i = 5;  double d = i / 2;  the value of d is:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: i / 2 is evaluated as integer division (2) before conversion to double.

questions.question: In C, what is printed by  char c = 'A' + 2;  printf("%c", c); ?
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects

questions.question: Which conversion is a narrowing conversion that may lose information?
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: The fractional part (and possibly range) is lost; the others widen.

questions.question: Under structural type equivalence, two types are equivalent if:

options.A: They are declared on the same line
options.C: They have the same structure, even if their names differ
options.D: They have the same name only

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Name equivalence requires the same type name; structural equivalence compares components.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a purpose of declarations (Pratt)?

options.B: Enabling static type checking and resolving overloaded operations
options.D: Storage management information such as lifetime

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Declarations help storage representation, storage management, polymorphic/overloaded operations and static type checking.

questions.question: A binding that occurs before run time and remains unchanged throughout execution is called:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Dynamic binding happens or can change during execution.

questions.question: The specification of a data type consists of:

options.A: Its attributes, the values its objects may take and the operations defined on them

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: The implementation then gives storage representation and algorithms for the operations.

questions.question: A run-time descriptor (dope vector) of a data object stores:

options.A: Its attributes, such as type, bounds and size, needed during execution
options.C: The source code of the object

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: E.g. an array descriptor holds its bounds and element size for subscript checking.

questions.question: The specification  + : integer × integer → integer  is called the operation's:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: A signature gives the domain (argument types) and range (result type).

questions.question: An operation that modifies one of its arguments in addition to returning a result is said to have a:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: E.g. x++ returns a value and also changes x.

questions.question: A dangling reference is:

options.A: A pointer that is always NULL
options.B: A data object with no access path left
options.C: An access path that still exists to a data object that has been deallocated

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: The reverse situation – an object with no access path – is garbage.

questions.question: When two names in a program refer to the same data object at the same time, this is called:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: E.g. passing the same variable twice by reference.

questions.question: In ML or Haskell, the compiler can find the types of most expressions without declarations. This is called:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Hindley–Milner type inference deduces types statically.

questions.question:
Match the category of variable with the time its storage is bound:
a. Static
b. Stack-dynamic
c. Explicit heap-dynamic
d. Implicit heap-dynamic

1. Created by new / malloc
2. When a value is assigned, e.g. in Python
3. For the whole program run
4. When its declaration is elaborated on subprogram entry
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Sebesta's four categories of variables by lifetime.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Dynamic type checking gives the programmer more flexibility.
Reason (R): With dynamic type checking, type information has to be kept with each data object at run time.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Both true; R states a cost of dynamic checking, not the reason for its flexibility.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): C performs complete static type checking.
Reason (R): C unions allow the same storage to be read as different types without any check.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Unchecked unions (and casts) mean C's static checking is incomplete; R shows why A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Coercions can reduce the reliability of programs.
Reason (R): Implicit conversions can hide type errors that the compiler would otherwise report.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: E.g. mistyping a float variable for an int one goes unnoticed when coercion is allowed.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A dangling reference arises when storage is freed while a pointer still refers to it.
Reason (R): Garbage collection is the main cause of dangling references.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: A is true. R is false: garbage collection frees only unreachable objects, so it prevents dangling references.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. An r-value is the value stored in a data object.
II. A named constant has an l-value that can be the target of an assignment.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: A constant's value cannot be changed by assignment, so II is false.

questions.question: In Python,  x = 5  followed by  x = 'hello'  is legal because:

options.B: x is declared as a string
options.D: Python binds types to values dynamically at assignment

questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: The variable is only a name; its type follows the object it currently refers to.

questions.question: Using + for both integer and floating-point addition is an example of:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: The same operator symbol stands for different operations chosen by operand types.

questions.question: In a statically typed language, the type of a variable is bound at:
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Static typing = types known and checked before execution.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The scope of a variable is a textual (static) property.
II. The lifetime of a variable is a temporal (run-time) property.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Properties of Types and Objects
questions.explanation: Scope = region of program text where the name is visible; lifetime = time during which storage exists. A static local in C has local scope but whole-program lifetime.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a scalar data type?
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: A scalar object holds a single value; a string is a composite of characters.

questions.question: The range of a 16-bit two's-complement integer is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: n bits give −2ⁿ⁻¹ to 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1.

questions.question: The range of an 8-bit unsigned integer is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: 2⁸ = 256 values starting from 0.

questions.question: The 8-bit two's-complement representation of −5 is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types

questions.question: A subrange type such as 1..10 in Pascal offers which advantages?

options.D: Less storage and automatic range checking

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Values can be packed in fewer bits and out-of-range assignments are detected.

questions.question: In C, given  enum colour {RED, GREEN = 5, BLUE};  the value of BLUE is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: RED = 0, GREEN = 5 explicitly, BLUE = GREEN + 1 = 6.

questions.question: A Boolean value needs only one bit, but it is usually stored in a whole byte because:

options.B: The byte is normally the smallest addressable unit of memory

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Accessing single bits needs extra masking operations.

questions.question: In C, the value of  '7' − '0'  is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Digit characters have consecutive codes: 55 − 48 = 7.

questions.question: In IEEE 754 single precision, the fields are:

options.A: 1 sign bit, 7 exponent bits, 24 fraction bits
options.B: 8 sign bits, 8 exponent bits, 16 fraction bits
options.C: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits, 52 fraction bits
options.D: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 fraction bits

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Total 32 bits; the second option is double precision.

questions.question: The exponent bias used in IEEE 754 single precision is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Double precision uses 1023.

questions.question: In IEEE 754 single precision, the stored (biased) exponent field of the number 1.0 is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types

questions.question: Comparing two floating-point values with == is risky because:

options.A: Many decimal fractions such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary
options.C: The == operator is illegal for floats
options.D: Floating values are always rounded to integers

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false in binary floating point; compare with a tolerance.

questions.question: Fixed-point decimal representation is preferred for:

options.A: Scientific calculations with very large ranges
options.C: Money and business calculations that need exact decimal digits

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: COBOL and PL/I provide fixed-point decimal types for this reason.

questions.question: In C,  strlen("hello")  and  sizeof("hello")  are respectively:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: sizeof counts the terminating '\0'; strlen does not.

questions.question: A file differs from most other data objects because:

options.B: It is always stored in registers
options.D: It resides on secondary storage and its lifetime can be longer than the program that created it

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Pratt: files are the usual way data persists between program runs.

questions.question: An array is ______, whereas a record (structure) is ______.
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Array elements share one type; record fields can have different types.

questions.question: A[10][20] is stored in row-major order from base address 1000, with 4 bytes per element and 0-based indices. The address of A[5][6] is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types

questions.question: A[1..10, 1..20] is stored in column-major order from base address 2000, with 2 bytes per element. The address of A[3, 4] is:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Columns before: (4 − 1) × 10 = 30; rows before in its column: 3 − 1 = 2; 2000 + 32 × 2 = 2064.

questions.question: How many elements does the array A[−2..5, 3..7] have?
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types

questions.question: The size of a C union is (ignoring padding):

options.A: The size of its first member
options.C: The size of its largest member
options.D: The sum of the sizes of its members

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: All members share the same storage.

questions.question: A Pascal-style  set of 0..31  is most efficiently implemented as:

options.D: A 32-bit string with one bit per possible element

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Union and intersection then become bitwise OR and AND.

questions.question:
Match the type with its usual storage representation:
a. Boolean
b. Character
c. Floating-point
d. Set (small base type)

1. Sign, exponent and mantissa
2. A single bit or byte
3. A code such as ASCII or Unicode

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Standard representations described in Pratt, chapter on elementary data types.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Subrange types can improve program reliability.
Reason (R): The translator or run-time system can check that assigned values stay within the declared range.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Range checks catch errors that would otherwise produce wrong values silently.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Floating-point numbers can represent every real number within their range exactly.
Reason (R): They use a fixed, finite number of bits for the mantissa.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: With finitely many bits only finitely many values are representable; R explains why A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): In C, an array name used in an expression usually converts to a pointer to its first element.
Reason (R): C arrays store their length as part of the array object.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: A is true (array-to-pointer decay). R is false: C arrays carry no length, which is why functions need a size argument.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Enumeration types make programs more readable.
Reason (R): Enumeration values are usually stored internally as small integers.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Both true, but readability comes from meaningful names, not from the internal integer representation.

questions.question:
Consider the statements about a C union:
I. It can hold valid values of all its members at the same time.
II. Storing into one member can change the value read through another member.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Members overlap in memory, so only the last stored member is meaningful.

questions.question: To keep a student's name, roll number and marks together as one data object, the most suitable type is a:
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Fields of different types are grouped in a record.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. A pointer data object holds the location (address) of another data object.
II. In C, dereferencing a NULL pointer is always detected at compile time.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: II is false: a NULL dereference is a run-time error (undefined behaviour) that the compiler usually cannot detect.

questions.question: Which operation is NOT normally defined on an enumeration type such as {MON, TUE, WED}?
questions.subject: Scalar and Composite Data Types
questions.explanation: Enumerations are ordered, so comparison and succ/pred make sense; arithmetic like MON × TUE does not.

questions.question: Which of the following is a valid C identifier?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: Identifiers start with a letter or underscore, contain only letters, digits and underscores, and cannot be keywords.

questions.question: How many keywords does ANSI C (C89) define?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: C89 has 32 keywords; C99 added 5 more (inline, restrict, _Bool, _Complex, _Imaginary).

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a C token?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: Comments are removed before tokenisation (replaced by a space); tokens are keywords, identifiers, constants, string literals, operators and punctuators.

questions.question: What does  printf("%d", 0x1F);  print?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: In C a character constant has type int; in C++ it has type char.

questions.question: sizeof(char) in C is:
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: The standard defines sizeof(char) as 1 byte.

questions.question: The range of a signed char (8-bit, two's complement) is:
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: 8 bits give 256 values: −2⁷ to 2⁷ − 1.

questions.question: With 32-bit int, what does  unsigned int x = -1;  printf("%u", x);  print?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: −1 converted to unsigned wraps to 2³² − 1.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In C, overflow of an unsigned integer wraps around modulo 2ⁿ.
II. In C, overflow of a signed int is guaranteed to wrap around the same way.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: Unsigned arithmetic is modular by definition; signed overflow is undefined behaviour.

questions.question: In C, the constant 3.14 has type:
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: Floating constants are double unless suffixed: 3.14f is float, 3.14L is long double.

questions.question: What is  strlen("a\tb")?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.question: To read a double with scanf, the correct format specifier is:
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.question: What does  char c = 65;  printf("%c %d", c, c);  print?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.question: In C,  Sum  and  sum  are:
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: C is case-sensitive.

options.D: Compile-time error: assignment to a read-only variable

questions.explanation: A const-qualified object is not a modifiable l-value.

questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.question: What does  printf("%x", 255);  print?

questions.question: On a typical system,  sizeof(3.0)  is:
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types
questions.explanation: 3.0 is a double constant.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a data-type modifier in C?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Whether plain char is signed or unsigned is implementation-defined.
II. sizeof(int) is always 2 bytes in C.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Tokens, Identifiers and Data Types

options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: Because the type is unknown, the compiler cannot dereference it; R shows why A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): calloc() initialises the allocated memory to zero.
Reason (R): malloc() takes a single argument, the number of bytes.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: Both true, but malloc's signature does not explain calloc's zero-initialisation.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. Returning the address of a local (automatic) variable from a function creates a dangling pointer.
II. Memory from malloc() is freed automatically when the calling function returns.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: Heap memory lives until free() is called; locals die when the function returns.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. The name of an array is a constant pointer and cannot be incremented (a++ is illegal).
II. A pointer variable set to the array can be incremented (p++ is legal).
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: a is not a modifiable l-value, but p is an ordinary variable.

questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: Both **q and *p are x: 10 + 10.

questions.question: The standard library function used to change the size of a block previously allocated by malloc is:
questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: realloc may move the block and returns its new address.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. malloc() returns NULL if the requested memory cannot be allocated.
II. Calling free() twice on the same pointer is safe.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: Pointers
questions.explanation: A double free is undefined behaviour and can corrupt the heap.

sets.name: 2 · File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors

questions.question: Opening a file with fopen(name, "w") when the file already exists:

options.B: Truncates it to zero length and writes from the beginning

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Use "a" to append or "r+" to update without truncating.

questions.question: fopen() returns ______ if the file cannot be opened.
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Always test the returned FILE pointer before using it.

questions.question: The FILE type and functions such as fopen and fprintf are declared in:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: stdio = standard input/output.

questions.question: To write one structure variable rec to a binary file fp, the correct call is:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: fwrite(pointer, size of each item, number of items, stream).

questions.question: After  fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_END);  the call  ftell(fp)  returns:

options.A: The size of the file in bytes

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: The position at the end equals the file length (for binary streams).

questions.question: rewind(fp) is equivalent to:

options.D: fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET) (and clearing the error indicator)

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: It moves the position back to the start.

questions.question: fclose(fp) is important because it:

options.B: Moves to the end of the file
options.D: Flushes buffered output to the file and releases the stream

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Unflushed data may be lost if a program ends abnormally without closing.

questions.question: The three standard streams opened automatically for a C program are:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: stderr is unbuffered, so error messages appear immediately.

questions.question: A program is run as  ./prog one two .  In main(int argc, char *argv[]), argc and argv[2] are:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: argv[0] is the program name, so there are 3 arguments.

questions.question: In main(int argc, char *argv[]), the element argv[argc] is:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: The standard guarantees argv[argc] == NULL.

questions.question: To convert the command-line argument "25" in argv[1] to an int, a program can use:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Casting the pointer gives an address, not the number; strtol is a safer alternative.

questions.question: With  #define SQUARE(x) x * x ,  what is the value of  SQUARE(2 + 3) ?
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: It expands to 2 + 3 * 2 + 3 = 11; arguments are substituted as text.

questions.question: If the macro is written with full parentheses as  #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x)) ,  then  SQUARE(2 + 3)  evaluates to:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Parentheses keep the argument together: (5) * (5).

questions.question: With  #define CUBE(x) (x * x * x) ,  what is the value of  CUBE(1 + 1) ?
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors

questions.question: Preprocessing happens:

options.B: Before compilation proper, on the source text

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Directives beginning with # are handled by the preprocessor.

questions.question: The difference between  #include <file.h>  and  #include "file.h"  is that:

options.A: The quoted form includes only the first line
options.C: The angle-bracket form searches only the current directory
options.D: The quoted form searches the current (source) directory first, then the system directories

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Angle brackets are used for standard/system headers.

questions.question: Include guards such as  #ifndef MY_H  #define MY_H … #endif  are used to:

options.A: Prevent a header's contents from being processed twice in one translation unit
options.C: Hide the header from the compiler

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Double inclusion would cause redefinition errors.

questions.question: With  #define STR(x) #x ,  STR(hello) expands to:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: # is the stringizing operator.

questions.question: With  #define JOIN(a, b) a##b ,  JOIN(x, 1) expands to:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: ## is the token-pasting operator.

questions.question: Which of the following is a predefined macro in ANSI C?
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: __FILE__, __LINE__, __DATE__, __TIME__ and __STDC__ are predefined.

questions.question: #undef NAME is used to:

options.B: Remove a previous macro definition of NAME

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: NAME can then be redefined.

questions.question: With  #define MAX(a, b) ((a) > (b) ? (a) : (b)) ,  int i = 5, j = 3;  and  m = MAX(i++, j); , the final value of i is:
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: i++ appears twice in the expansion and is evaluated twice because i > j – a classic macro side-effect trap.

questions.question:
Match the function with its action:
a. fseek
b. ftell
c. rewind
d. feof

1. Moves the position to a chosen place
2. Returns non-zero after an attempt to read past the end
3. Moves the position to the beginning
4. Returns the current file position
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: All take a FILE * argument.

questions.question:
Match the fopen mode with its meaning:
a. "r"
b. "w"
c. "a"

1. Read an existing file
2. Read and update an existing file

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Adding b (e.g. "rb") opens the file in binary mode.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): The value returned by fgetc() should be stored in an int, not a char.
Reason (R): fgetc() returns EOF, a value distinct from every valid character.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: A char cannot reliably hold both all 256 byte values and EOF (−1).

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Opening an existing file in "w" mode appends new data to its end.
Reason (R): The "a" mode opens a file for appending.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: "w" truncates; appending is what "a" does, which shows A is false.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Include guards prevent a header from being included twice in a translation unit.
Reason (R): The preprocessor runs before the compiler proper.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: Both true, but the guard works because of the #ifndef/#define test, not merely because preprocessing comes first.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): Macros can be faster than functions for very small operations.
Reason (R): Macro arguments are type-checked by the compiler just like function arguments.

options.A: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.B: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.C: A is true, but R is false
options.D: A is false, but R is true

questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: A is true (no call overhead). R is false: macros are plain text substitution with no type checking.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. argv[0] normally holds the name used to run the program.
II. argc counts only the arguments after the program name.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: argc includes the program name, so argc ≥ 1.

questions.question:
Consider the statements:
I. In text mode, newline characters may be translated on some systems (for example to CR-LF on Windows).
II. In binary mode, bytes are read and written without any translation.
Which is/are correct?
questions.subject: File Handling, Command Line Arguments and Preprocessors
questions.explanation: This is why binary data must be written to files opened with "wb".
